::: {.callout-note appearance="simple" icon=false}
## TL;DR

When treatment is assigned by whether a continuous score $X$ crosses a threshold $c$ (a passing grade, an income cutoff, or a spatial boundary), units just below and just above $c$ are nearly identical except for treatment. **Sharp regression discontinuity design (RDD)** estimates the causal effect $\tau$ as the vertical jump between two local regressions fitted on either side of $c$. Always check sensitivity to bandwidth and cutoff placement—a true threshold effect peaks sharply at $c$ rather than appearing everywhere along $X$.
:::

## The intuition: comparing just above and just below

Suppose units receive an intervention whenever a running variable $X_i \ge c$. Because units cannot precisely manipulate their score right around $c$, comparing $X_i = c - \epsilon$ with $X_i = c + \epsilon$ approximates a local randomized experiment.

We fit separate linear models to the left ($X_i < c$) and right ($X_i \ge c$) of the cutoff:

$$Y_i = \alpha + \tau D_i + \beta_1 (X_i - c) + \beta_2 D_i (X_i - c) + \varepsilon_i$$

where $D_i = \mathbb{1}(X_i \ge c)$ is the treatment indicator, $\alpha$ is the left-hand intercept at the cutoff, and $\tau$ is the estimated **discontinuity jump** at $X = c$:

$$\hat{\tau} = \lim_{x \downarrow c} \hat{\mathbb{E}}[Y \mid X = x] - \lim_{x \uparrow c} \hat{\mathbb{E}}[Y \mid X = x]$$

## Sweeping cutoffs as a diagnostic check

In exploratory data, you may want to verify whether a discontinuity appears at a known threshold $c$ rather than at arbitrary points along $X$. Sweeping candidate cutoffs $c \in [c_{\min}, c_{\max}]$ and computing the predicted jump at each $c$ reveals whether the jump is localized or just curvature in the underlying relationship.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## View R code: fitting left/right linear models and sweeping cutoffs

```r
library(tidyverse)

# respRatio.RDS is not included. Any data frame with columns env, resp, pos.raw
# and respRatio.byEnv works.
df <- readRDS("respRatio.RDS")

# Sweep candidate cutoffs across environments
results <- map_dfr(1:20, function(e) {
  sub_df <- df %>% filter(resp == 1, env == e)

  map_dfr(seq(5.5, 25.5, by = 1), function(cutoff) {
    right <- lm(respRatio.byEnv ~ pos.raw, data = filter(sub_df, pos.raw > cutoff))
    left  <- lm(respRatio.byEnv ~ pos.raw, data = filter(sub_df, pos.raw < cutoff))

    jump <- predict(right, newdata = data.frame(pos.raw = cutoff)) -
            predict(left,  newdata = data.frame(pos.raw = cutoff))

    tibble(env = e, cutoff = cutoff, jump = unname(jump))
  })
})

# Plot raw points, split linear fits at c = 12.5, and |jump| curve
df %>%
  filter(resp == 1) %>%
  mutate(group = cut(pos.raw, breaks = c(1, 12.5, 30), include.lowest = TRUE)) %>%
  ggplot(aes(x = pos.raw, y = respRatio.byEnv, color = group)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.6) +
  geom_smooth(method = "lm", se = FALSE) +
  geom_line(data = results, aes(x = cutoff, y = abs(jump)), inherit.aes = FALSE, color = "black") +
  facet_wrap(~env)
```
:::

## Key assumptions and pitfalls

1. **No manipulation of $X$:** Units must not be able to sort themselves just above $c$ (check for bunching in the histogram of $X$ around $c$).
2. **Functional form:** Fitting a straight line across a wide range can mistake a smooth curve for a jump at $c$; restrict to a local bandwidth around $c$ or use local polynomial regression (`rdrobust`).
3. **Placebo cutoffs:** If candidate cutoffs far from $c$ produce jumps of similar magnitude, the apparent discontinuity is likely model misspecification rather than a causal effect.

## Key takeaways

- Sharp RDD identifies the **local average treatment effect at the cutoff $c$**, not across the entire range of $X$.
- Center the running variable at $(X_i - c)$ and allow different slopes on each side of the threshold.
- Validate any claimed jump with **bandwidth sensitivity** and **placebo cutoff** checks.
